Henry Knox. A Boston bookseller who rose to become the chief artillery officer of the Continental Army and one of the war's most technically proficient commanders. Self-taught in military science and engineering, he revolutionized American artillery tactics and later served as the nation's first Secretary of War.

Knox joined the Continental Army as a volunteer and quickly impressed George Washington with his mastery of artillery theory, earning promotion to Major General despite his lack of formal military training. He designed and supervised the construction of fortifications and siege works throughout the war, including the crucial defensive positions at Valley Forge and the siege works at Yorktown.

He reorganized and standardized American artillery practices, transforming cannons from inaccurate support weapons into precision instruments that could decide battles. At Yorktown in 1781, his artillery barrage helped force the British surrender and end the war.

Knox marched with Washington into defeated New York and served as his trusted aide-de-camp, becoming one of the general's most loyal subordinates. After the war, he became the first Secretary of War under the Constitution, where he modernized American military organization and founded the artillery corps that persists today.
